content: Naphazoline is an alpha-adrenergic agonist that has been approved by the FDA for use as a topical ocular vasoconstrictor. It is commonly used to reduce redness in the eyes. For adults, the recommended dosage is one or two drops instilled into the conjunctival sac(s) every three to four hours as needed. There is limited information available regarding off-label uses of naphazoline in adults. Similarly, there is insufficient data on its use in pediatric patients, both for FDA-approved and off-label indications. Naphazoline is contraindicated in individuals with anatomically narrow angles, narrow-angle glaucoma, or hypersensitivity to any of its components. Patients taking monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) are at risk of severe hypertensive crises if they use naphazoline or other sympathomimetic drugs. In children, particularly infants, the drug may cause central nervous system depression, potentially leading to coma and a significant drop in body temperature. This medication is intended for topical ophthalmic use only. It should be used cautiously in patients with hypertension, cardiovascular disorders, diabetes (hyperglycemia), hyperthyroidism, or in the presence of infection or injury. Systemic side effects such as dizziness, headache, nausea, sweating, nervousness, drowsiness, weakness, hypertension, cardiac irregularities, and hyperglycemia have also been observed. Drug interactions are a concern with naphazoline. Concurrent use with maprotiline or tricyclic antidepressants may enhance its pressor effects. Patients on MAOIs are at particular risk of severe hypertensive crises when using naphazoline. In pregnancy, naphazoline is classified as Category C by the FDA, meaning that animal reproduction studies have not been conducted, and its effects on human pregnancy are unknown. It should only be used during pregnancy if clearly necessary. There is no information on its excretion in human milk, so caution is advised when administering it to nursing mothers. Its safety and efficacy in pediatric and geriatric populations have not been established. The mechanism of action of naphazoline involves constriction of the conjunctival blood vessels, likely through direct stimulation of alpha-adrenergic receptors in the arterioles. This reduces conjunctival congestion. Naphazoline is a sympathomimetic amine and an imidazoline derivative. The drug is supplied as a sterile 0.1% ophthalmic solution in 15 mL plastic dropper bottles. It should be stored at a temperature of 20° to 25°C (68° to 77°F) and kept tightly closed. Patients should be instructed to discontinue use and consult a physician if symptoms persist or worsen after 48 hours, or if systemic symptoms such as dizziness, headache, nausea, drowsiness, or a drop in body temperature occur. To avoid contamination, the dropper tip should not touch any surfaces, including the eyelids or surrounding areas. If the solution changes color or becomes cloudy, it should not be used. There is no established interaction between alcohol and naphazoline, but patients should consult their healthcare provider regarding alcohol consumption while using this medication. The drug is marketed under the brand name AK-Con®.
